paper_title: FinForesight: A Diagnostic Backtesting Benchmark for Deep Research Systems in Financial Forecasting

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Anticipating financial outcomes requires synthesizing evolving evidence and reasoning under uncertainty, making deep research systems promising tools for forecasting. Yet evaluating forecasting ability is challenging because historical backtests may reward memorized outcomes or information retrieved after the forecast date. Live forecasting avoids direct access to realized outcomes, but feedback arrives only after events resolve. To obtain timely feedback and assess historical scores, we introduce FinForesight, a diagnostic backtesting benchmark for financial deep research systems. Across the Chinese, U.S., and Hong Kong markets, the benchmark evaluates four forecasting tasks: valuation, return ranking, event direction, and future financial fundamentals. Two capability diagnostic tasks assess counterfactual reasoning and financial calculation, scored separately from forecasting performance. Our harness-compatible framework restricts retrieved evidence to information available at the forecast date. We compare pretraining-era, resolved post-cutoff, and live evaluations to test whether controlled backtests approximate future performance. Pretraining-era scores exceed post-cutoff scores in most temporal comparisons, and stronger retrieval controls narrow the gap between post-cutoff backtests and live results. Forecasting attribution and robustness analyses reveal how scores respond to retrieval policy and how predictions respond to prompt rewrites and numerical perturbations. The code and benchmark data are publicly available.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Financial forecasting requires anticipating how companies and markets will respond to new information. Such judgments draw on historical prices, corporate disclosures, and news, including evidence that price trends alone cannot capture. *Equal contribution. Corresponding author. 1 Figure 1: Can controlled T2 backtests approximate T3 forecasting performance? The model knowledge cutoff cm marks the T1/T2 boundary, and the benchmark run date marks the T2/T3 boundary. T1 contains pretraining-era history, T2 resolved post-cutoff events, and T3 unresolved live events. Evidence used for each forecast must have been public by the prediction time t. Deep research systems can gather time-sensitive evidence and synthesize it through multi-step reasoning, making them promising for such forecasts (Li et al., 2025b; MiroMind Team et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a). In finance, FinRobot integrates financial data and qualitative analysis to produce financial projections and valuation reports (Zhou et al., 2024). Fin-DR further combines multi-turn evidence retrieval with financial time-series forecasting in deep research workflow (Duan et al., 2026). As these workflows are used for forward-looking analysis, reliably evaluating their predictive ability becomes increasingly important for financial research and investment decisions. Historical backtests can be scored immediately, but model may already know the outcome it is asked to predict. Live evaluation records forecasts before outcomes resolve, but provides feedback only after the events occur. Figure 1 places these approaches across three regimes defined by the model knowledge cutoff cm and benchmark run date r. In T1, historical outcomes may have appeared in training data, allowing parametric memory to appear as forecasting ability (Li et al., 2026c). In T2, forecast dates follow the knowledge cutoff and outcomes are resolved by the run date, making scores immediately available without the same pretraining-era exposure. Yet retrieval leakage can expose published outcomes or other evidence unavailable at the original forecast date, even when search date filters are applied (Lahib et al., 2026). T3 contains live events whose outcomes remain unresolved at the run date and can be scored only after resolution. This leaves tradeoff between timely backtest feedback and direct but delayed live validation. Existing forecasting benchmarks broadly adopt two approaches: live forecasting and pastcasting. Live forecasting records predictions before outcomes are resolved, as in ForecastBench (Karger et al., 2024), FutureX (Zeng et al., 2025), and the finance-focused FinDeepForecast (Li et al., 2026b). In contrast, Wildman et al. (2025) introduce Bench to the Future (BTF), pastcasting benchmark that reconstructs historical evidence for resolved questions, enabling immediate evaluation. This creates need to compare controlled historical backtests directly with live forecasting outcomes in financial markets. Interpreting their scores also requires examining historical knowledge, retrieval leakage, and sensitivity to prompt formulations and numerical inputs. This leads to our central question: Can Historical Backtests Reliably Evaluate Deep Research for Financial Forecasting? To address this question, we introduce FinForesight, diagnostic backtesting benchmark for financial deep research systems. It spans the Chinese, U.S., and Hong Kong markets and assesses four forecasting targets: stock valuation, relative return ranking, event direction, and future financial fundamentals. Two capability diagnostic tasks assess counterfactual reasoning and financial calculation, with scores reported separately from the forecasting score. We generate instances relative to each models knowledge cutoff and use resolved T2 events to provide timely feedback. timecontrolled framework supports multiple deep research harnesses and restricts retrieved evidence to information available at the forecast date. We compare controlled T2 scores with live T3 scores to assess how well historical backtests reflect live forecasting performance. To interpret these scores, we compare temporal regimes and retrieval policies for signs of memory or information leakage. Prompt rewrites and numerical perturbations reveal how predictions respond to changes in task wording and numerical inputs. Our experiments reveal substantial differences across temporal regimes and forecasting tasks. Pretraining-era evaluations show widespread historical score advantages, and stronger retrieval controls bring T2 backtest scores closer to live results. Controlled T2 evaluation therefore offers timely feedback for model and system development. Diagnostic analyses expose sensitivities to information access and input formulation that aggregate forecasting scores alone cannot capture. Across modelharness configurations, the finance-specific workflow does not consistently outperform generalpurpose alternatives. Together, these findings show why forecasting scores must be interpreted alongside the conditions under which they are obtained. The main contributions of this work are: We build benchmark spanning four forecasting tasks and two capability diagnostic tasks across the Chinese, U.S., and Hong Kong markets, with resolved T2 events enabling timely evaluation. We develop time-controlled evaluation framework compatible with multiple deep research harnesses that generates instances relative to model knowledge cutoffs and audits retrieved evidence against forecast dates. We analyze forecasting attribution and robustness through temporal comparisons, retrieval-policy tests, prompt rewrites, and numerical perturbations to investigate the sources of apparent forecasting performance.

sections.title: Validity
sections.content: Live forecasting records predictions before outcomes resolve but delays evaluation until outcomes become observable (Karger et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2025). Pastcasting avoids this delay by evaluating resolved questions against reconstructed historical evidence. Related approaches use frozen retrieval environments for reproducible research-agent evaluation or replay historical prediction markets for retrospective forecasting (FutureSearch et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026). Pastcasting studies also compare retrospective evaluations with live forecasting performance (Wildman et al., 2025; Chai et al., 2026). However, whether controlled historical backtests reliably reflect live forecasting performance across financial tasks remains unclear. Historical forecasting evaluation also faces risks of temporal information leakage. Models may recall historical financial outcomes, and instructions to disregard future knowledge may fail to prevent 2 their use (Didisheim et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026c). Date-filtered retrieval may also expose information unavailable at the original forecast date, motivating explicit look-ahead audits (Lahib et al., 2026; Benhenda, 2026). FinForesight combines model-cutoffaware temporal partitioning with point-in-time retrieval auditing to address these risks in financial deep research evaluation. It uses T1T2 comparisons to probe historical performance advantages and T2T3 comparisons under different retrieval policies to assess backtest-to-live agreement. 2.2 Financial Agent Benchmarks Existing financial-agent benchmarks assess diverse capabilities, including filing-based research, expert investment judgments, and financial decisionmaking (Bigeard et al., 2025; Cho et al., 2026; Li et al., 2024). FinTradeBench (Agrawal et al., 2026) examines reasoning over fundamental and technical trading signals. DeepFund (Li et al., 2025a) and related benchmarks evaluate investment decisions in market environments (Qian et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). Code-based alpha discovery represents another evaluation setting for financial research agents (Liu et al., 2026b,a). However, aggregate scores across diverse financial tasks may obscure performance on specific future-outcome forecasting tasks. FinForesight therefore evaluates valuation, return ranking, event direction, and future financial fundamentals separately across three markets using task-specific outcome-based scores. Beyond forecasting accuracy, understanding why systems perform well and whether their predictions are reliable requires complementary diagnostics. KTD-Fin (Zhu et al., 2026) investigates the decomposition of trading returns. Related work examines code validity, numerical reasoning, and prompt-dependent forecasting behavior (Luo et al., 2026; Levy, 2026; Tang et al., 2025; Schoenegger et al., 2025). FinForesight uses temporal comparisons and retrieval interventions to investigate historical performance advantages and retrieval sensitivity. Counterfactual reasoning and financial calculation serve as capability diagnostic tasks. Prompt rewrites and numerical perturbations assess the robustness of forecasting predictions.

sections.title: 3.1 Preliminaries
sections.content: Evaluation setup. We evaluate the forecasting performance and supporting capabilities of complete modelharness systems under controlled information conditions. Each instance provides question and task-specific inputs, and the systems response is compared against reference label accessible only to the evaluator. Temporal setup. Let cm denote the models declared knowledge cutoff, the instances forecast date, and the benchmark run date. In historical backtests, is the simulated forecast date. Let It denote information verifiably public by t. In time-controlled runs, supplied inputs and retrieved evidence are restricted to It. For outcome-based tasks, Figure 1 distinguishes: T1: Pretraining-era historical events. Both the forecast date and outcome resolution precede cm, so realized outcomes may have been encountered during pretraining. T2: Post-cutoff resolved events. The forecast date follows cm, and outcomes resolve between and r, enabling immediate scoring. T3: Live future events. Predictions are recorded before outcomes resolve, with reference labels becoming available only after r. Design principles. We adopt four principles to support forecasting evaluation, attribution, and robustness analysis. Temporal control beyond prompts. We enforce point-in-time information access and use temporal comparisons to probe potential historical knowledge effects (Li et al., 2026c). Page-level retrieval audits. We audit retrieved content against the forecast date, since timestamps and search filters alone cannot guarantee temporal validity (Lahib et al., 2026). Decomposed evaluation. We report performance separately by task, market, and temporal regime to distinguish forecasting capabilities and support diagnostic comparisons. Response robustness. We use prompt rewrites to assess prediction consistency and numerical perturbations to examine sensitivity to input changes (Schoenegger et al., 2025; Levy, 2026).

sections.title: 3.2 Benchmark
sections.content: Benchmark construction. We construct FinForesight dynamically across six task families and the Chinese, U.S., and Hong Kong markets, adapting instances to each models knowledge cutoff. Task templates generate questions, required inputs, 3 Figure 2: Three-stage workflow of FinForesight. Model-specific instances are constructed across financial tasks, markets, and T1/T2/T3 temporal regimes. The modelharness system generates predictions using only external information available at the forecast date. The evaluator scores predictions against reference labels immediately for resolved outcomes or after resolution for live events. Temporal comparisons assess historical performance advantages and backtest-to-live agreement, and prompt perturbations examine prediction robustness. and answer schemas, with target dates and prediction windows constrained by the applicable temporal conditions. We retain candidates with sufficient inputs and reproducible reference-label rules. We verify evidence timestamps and confirm that the information was publicly available by t. Forecasting labels are derived from subsequently realized market or financial outcomes, whereas capability diagnostic answers follow predefined logical or computational rules. T3 labels are added after the corresponding outcomes resolve. Market prices are obtained from Yahoo Finance (Yahoo Finance, n.d.). Filings and financial values are collected from SEC EDGAR, CNINFO, the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges, and HKEXnews (U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, n.d.; CNINFO, n.d.; Shanghai Stock Exchange, n.d.; Shenzhen Stock Exchange, n.d.; Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, n.d.). Macroeconomic events are sourced from releases by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Chinas National Bureau of Statistics, and Hong Kongs Census and Statistics Department (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, n.d.; National Bureau of Statistics of China, n.d.; Census and Statistics Department, Hong Kong, n.d.). We compare systems on matched eligible instances to improve comparability across different model knowledge cutoffs. Source availability at the forecast date is verified independently of outcome-label collection. Task suite. Equity research involves assessing stock valuations, relative returns among industry peers, market reactions to events, and future financial performance. FinForesight evaluates these judgments through four forecasting tasks: Valuation (VAL), Return Ranking (RANK), Event Direction (EVT), and Fundamentals (FUND). Their reference labels are derived from realized outcomes, and their scores contribute to the overall forecasting score. Two capability diagnostic tasks, Counterfactual (CF) and Calculation (CALC), assess conditional reasoning and financial calculation, respectively. Their reference answers are predefined, and their scores are reported separately from the overall forecasting score. Appendix presents each tasks input, output, scoring rule, and example. Valuation (VAL). VAL forecasts stocks future price through bear, base, and bull targets, together with an expected time bucket for reaching the predicted range. Predictions use point-intime evidence and are evaluated against subsequent market prices. Return Ranking (RANK). RANK evaluates relative return forecasting by ranking industry peers according to their expected excess returns over specified horizon. It includes fundamental-only, 4 technical-only, and hybrid variants, with rankings compared against realized returns. Event Direction (EVT). EVT predicts market reactions to earnings, policy, and macroeconomic events using information available at the forecast date. The system outputs return direction and upward probability, evaluated against realized market movements. Fundamentals (FUND). FUND forecasts company financial metrics that have not yet been disclosed at the prediction date. Predicted values are compared with subsequent financial disclosures. Counterfactual (CF). CF assesses conditional reasoning through paired fictional announcements with contrasting financial implications. It tests whether predicted excess-return directions follow the supplied event conditions, including cases that conflict with historical price trends. Calculation (CALC). CALC evaluates multistep financial numerical reasoning using problems with distractor values and unit or convention traps. Intermediate calculations and final answers are checked against predefined references. Task example. The following example presents an abbreviated VAL task instance, its recorded price targets, and the held-out 30-day reference price. Additional task examples appear in Appendix A, where missing diagnostic records are highlighted in red. VAL: Wuliangye (000858), CN. Question. Using public information available before 202601-30, estimate bear, base, and bull price targets over 30-day forecast horizon. The price at the forecast date is CNY 105.00 per share. Recorded price targets. GPT-4.1-mini with GPTResearcher, using search, PIT control, and the LLM filter: bear base bull CNY 95.00 CNY 110.00 CNY 125.00 Held-out reference. The observed 30-day reference price is CNY 104.05 per share on 2026-02-27.

sections.title: 3.3 Time-Controlled Backtesting Framework
sections.content: Figure 2 illustrates the three-stage workflow used by FinForesight to evaluate modelharness systems, comprising benchmark construction, forecasting evaluation, and prediction attribution. For each eligible instance, the controller configures the specified model, harness, and retrieval policy before supplying task inputs. Reference labels remain accessible only to the evaluator. The harness accesses search, market data, and other tools through mediated services, with all interactions logged for subsequent evidence audits. We evaluate three retrieval policies: search without temporal checks, point-in-time (PIT) control, and PIT control augmented with an LLM-based leakage filter. System responses are recorded and locked before scoring. Resolved T1/T2 forecasts and capability diagnostic tasks are scored immediately, while T3 forecasts are scored after their outcomes resolve. Task scores follow the protocol in Section 4. Temporal comparisons and retrieval-policy interventions provide diagnostic evidence about historical performance advantages and the influence of external information. Prompt rewrites and numerical perturbations further examine prediction robustness. LLM leakage filter. PIT control uses source timestamps and available historical versions to restrict retrieved evidence to It, rejecting pages published after the forecast date t. We additionally use DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026), specifically its April 2026 release, as an LLMbased leakage filter over retrieved snippets and page content. The filter applies fixed classification prompt and decoding configuration across all runs to determine whether retrieved content was publicly available at t. Content containing post-t information, ambiguous temporal evidence, uncertain classifications, or invalid filter responses is rejected before reaching the evaluated system.

Task-specific forecast horizons, outcome resolution rules, and scoring criteria are detailed in Appendix A. Evaluation Metrics. VAL measures valuation error reduction relative to the cutoff-price baseline and reversion-horizon accuracy. sections.title: 4.3 Temporal Regime Analysis
sections.content: We compare GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini 3.1 FlashLite, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 in FinanceHarness on RANK, EVT, and FUND forecasting tasks. VAL is excluded from this focused analysis due to its sensitivity to short-horizon price fluctuations, with its temporal results reported in Table 5 in Appendix B. Table 3: US T2T3 score gaps across three retrieval settings in FinanceHarness, using matched one-week evaluation windows. Gaps are computed as T2 scores minus T3 scores, with positive values indicating higher T2 performance. Bold indicates the smallest absolute gap for each modeltask pair. Historical advantages are widespread. T1 scores exceed T2 scores in 25 of 27 comparisons across the three markets, including all RANK and FUND comparisons  (Table 2)  . The advantage appears across all three models, suggesting that each has memorized some historical outcomes (Didisheim et al., 2025). Pretraining-era backtests can therefore make recall look like prediction and should not be used alone to assess forecasting ability. Full scores appear in Table 5 in Appendix B. Temporal controls improve backtest-to-live agreement. We compare T2 and T3 scores over matched one-week windows under search only, point-in-time (PIT) control, and PIT plus an LLM leakage filter  (Table 3)  . With search alone, the mean absolute T2T3 gap across nine modeltask pairs is 0.1203. PIT lowers the mean gap to 0.0618, leaving gap that may reflect pages updated after the forecast date despite their earlier displayed timestamps (Lahib et al., 2026). Adding the LLM filter reduces the mean gap to 0.0285, approximately 76% below search alone, with smaller gaps in all nine comparisons. Under this stricter control, post-cutoff backtests closely approximate live forecasting scores in the evaluated tasks. Because T2 outcomes are already resolved, they provide timely feedback for model and system development. Full scores appear in Table 6.

sections.title: 4.5 Robustness and Sensitivity
sections.content: We assess input robustness on T2 EVT and FUND across CN, US, and HK using GPT-4.1-mini and Claude Sonnet 4.5 with FinanceHarness and GPTResearcher. Prompt variants rephrase the same question without changing its meaning or available evidence. Numerical variants slightly alter decimal precision, units, or nonessential values, with equivalent units accepted in scoring. Prompt Change Rate and Perturb Change Rate measure material changes in predictions, and Score Delta summarizes the mean signed score change across both interventions. Appendix reports aggregate results in Table 9 and taskmarket results in Table 10. Across the four modelharness configurations, Prompt Change Rates range from 16.83% to 23.67%, exceeding Perturb Change Rates of 7.00% to 9.17%. Both prompt wording and small numerical changes can alter individual predictions, with wording having the larger effect on outputs. Yet the mean signed Score Delta stays below 0.0026 in magnitude for every configuration, so these output changes have little effect on aggregate scores. This score stability supports task understanding across controlled input variations.

sections.title: 4.6 Prediction Attribution
sections.content: Table 4 combines temporal performance and input sensitivity for GPT-4.1-mini and Claude Sonnet 4.5 on US EVT and FUND in FinanceHarness. Both temporal gaps use T2 scores with search, pointin-time (PIT) control, and LLM filtering. The T3 column reports live forecasting scores directly. The final column reports the mean signed score change under prompt rewrites and numerical perturbations. All four T1 scores exceed their controlled T2 counterparts, suggesting an advantage from historical knowledge. Both models retain meaningful performance on live outcomes, with T3 scores of 0.58050.5926 on EVT and 0.71940.8563 on FUND. These scores indicate forecasting ability on events whose outcomes were unknown when the predictions were made. Filtered T2T3 gaps range from 0.0043 to 0.0267, supporting controlled T2 as close proxy for live scores in these four comparisons. Input Score Deltas remain below 0.004 in magnitude across all four comparisons, indicating small average score changes under prompt and numerical variants. Together, live performance, small filtered T2T3 gaps, and stable aggregate scores provide evidence that these models understand the forecasting tasks. The retrieval-policy scores appear in Appendix B.6.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced FinForesight with four forecasting and two capability diagnostic tasks across three markets, using time-controlled, multiharness framework. Strong capability scores do not ensure stronger forecasts, and T1s advantage over T2 points to historical knowledge effects. Model strengths vary across tasks and markets, and the finance-specific harness does not consistently outperform general-purpose workflows. In the matched one-week US experiment, PIT and filtering bring T2 backtests closer to live T3 scores, providing timely development feedback. Prompt rewrites and numerical perturbations alter some individual predictions, but have little effect on aggregate scores. For future work, we will test whether fresh T2 feedback helps autoresearch systems improve T3 forecasts, probing recursive selfimprovement (RSI) in finance.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: The benchmark has several limitations. First, point-in-time reconstruction is only an approximation: web pages, metadata, snippets, and archived sources may not perfectly match what an investor or deployed agent could access at the cutoff date. Second, CN, US, and HK markets differ in disclosure rules, language coverage, data vendors, and information-release timing, so cross-market results should be interpreted as diagnostic stability evidence rather than clean causal estimates of market difficulty. Third, T2 is practical retrospective proxy, not substitute for T3 live evaluation; the T2T3 relationship must be measured empirically.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: AI assistance in manuscript preparation was limited to grammar correction and refinement of logical clarity. All edits were reviewed by the authors, who take responsibility for the final manuscript.

B.4 Robustness Details Robustness results distinguish changes in individual predictions from changes in aggregate scores. Table 9 averages EVT and FUND results across CN, US, and HK for GPT-4.1-mini and Claude Sonnet 4.5 in two harnesses. For both models, FinanceHarness has lower Prompt and Perturb Change Rates than GPT-Researcher. Across the 24 taskmarket rows in Table 10, prompt rewrites change outputs more often than numerical perturbations. The difference is visible for GPT-4.1-mini on HK FUND with GPT-Researcher: its Prompt Change Rate is 0.35 and Perturb Change Rate is 0.10, with Score Delta of -0.0022592. All four aggregate Score Deltas have magnitude below 0.0026, showing that these response changes have much smaller effect on mean task scores. B.5 Capability Diagnostic Results CF tests supplied event logic and CALC tests stepwise calculation; Table 1 reports both scores for 22 configurations. Their scoring rules and examples appear in Appendix A. Within FinanceHarness, CF ranges from 0.9000 to 1.0000 across the three models in the temporal analysis. Across all configurations, CALC spans 0.2143 to 1.0000, showing greater variation in stepwise numerical reliability. Claude Sonnet 4.5 scores 1.0000 on both capability tasks with Claude Code, yet its forecasting Overall is 0.6292 there and 0.6797 with FinanceHarness. This contrast separates capability scores from future-outcome prediction. The comparison task-specific functions use direction changes for EVT/CF, rank distance for RANK, and numerical tolerances for VAL/FUND/CALC. Numerical comparison accounts for unit conversion and permissible response to genuine input changes; formula validity in CALC is checked against the appropriate reference, not literal expression identity. For CALC input perturbations, reference answers are recomputed, so correct numerical response is not penalized merely for differing from the original answer. T2T3 proximity.
